focus: Energy and commodity trade flows: what has broken in 2026 and where the barrels and cargoes went instead

routes.title: Strait of Hormuz effectively closed
routes.dateRange: Since late Feb / early Mar 2026, still live Oct 2026; attacks spiked early Oct and stayed elevated through mid-Oct
routes.summary: The US–Iran war has shut most commercial traffic through Hormuz for about eight months, with no durable diplomatic fix in sight. A June interim deal (the Islamabad MoU) briefly eased flows but collapsed; Iran now wants a return to it plus US backing for a separate Iran-Oman coordinated shipping-route deal, while Trump rejected Iran's latest seven-day reopening proposal. Attacks have stayed elevated rather than fading: Reuters counted at least 12 strikes on oil, LNG and LPG tankers in the week of 28 Sep-5 Oct, the highest weekly total since the war began, and UKMTO logged at least 11 further incidents in the Gulf between 11-14 October, including an Iranian-claimed strike on an ADNOC Logistics & Services VLCC. Harassment has widened beyond the strait itself to a container ship and sites off Qatar, Fujairah and Sohar, with the IRGC ordering at least one inbound tanker to turn back on 5 October. Yet despite the attacks, Kpler data show Middle East crude shipments through Hormuz recovered to roughly 80% of pre-war levels by September (~16 mb/d) as tankers sail on under US Navy-escorted convoys rather than diverting outright. For a trader, the questions are which barrels can still move (see the bypass pipelines entry), who replaces what doesn't (Atlantic Basin crude, Brazil, US, West Africa), and how freight and insurance reprice for ships that keep sailing into an active-strike zone.
routes.source: Reuters via gvwire (7 Oct 2026); Seatrade Maritime (2 & 13 Oct 2026); gCaptain (2 & 5 Oct 2026); Engine (15 Oct 2026); IEA Oil Market Report, Sep 2026; IMF PortWatch via straits.live, Oct 2026

events.title: Strait closes
events.text: US–Iran war begins and most commercial traffic through Hormuz stops. Pre-crisis norm: ~85 transits a day.

events.title: Tanker hit off Khasab
events.text: Oman's maritime security centre reported a tanker targeted ~5 nm north of Khasab port (Musandam). It was the first tanker attack of the war.
events.source: Oman Maritime Security Centre via Reuters (Mar 2026)

events.title: Iran's 'Strait Authority' blacklist
events.text: Iran's new Persian Gulf Strait Authority blacklisted 45 tankers in August for breaking its transit rules, and 56 by early September.

events.title: US naval escorts
events.text: US Navy escorts keep part of the flow moving. LNG carriers switch off AIS while crossing.

events.title: Oil flow 7.6 mb/d
events.text: IEA: oil through Hormuz averaged 7.6 mb/d in August, 13.1 mb/d below pre-war. Cumulative lost exports are approaching 2.8 bn barrels.

events.title: Partial recovery under escort
events.text: Kpler: Middle East crude shipments through Hormuz rose to ~80% of pre-war (~16 mb/d) in September with US Navy support.

events.title: ≥18 ships attacked
events.text: The FT counted at least 18 vessels attacked between 1 and 11 October, with European security sources recording 6 more. Transits fell to single digits on several days.

events.title: Outbound tanker hit, fire
events.text: UKMTO: an outbound tanker was struck on its port side by an unknown projectile and caught fire. Crew safe.

events.title: Tanker + 2 container ships hit
events.text: UKMTO: a tanker was struck by a projectile (Iran says it hit a mine after switching off its transponder), and two container ships were hit in separate incidents with minor damage.

routes.title: Hormuz bypass pipelines: Yanbu and Fujairah
routes.dateRange: Mar–Oct 2026; East-West line hit in early Sep
routes.summary: Only two pipelines get Gulf crude out without passing Hormuz. Saudi Arabia's East-West line to Yanbu on the Red Sea ramped up to about 5 mb/d (versus ~0.8 mb/d before the crisis), and the UAE's Habshan–Fujairah line exits below the strait. Analysts point to port loading capacity, not pipe capacity, as the binding limit. Then attacks shut the East-West pipeline in early September, cutting the main bypass. Barrels that do reach Yanbu must still pass a Red Sea where the Houthis are blockading Saudi-linked shipping (next entry), so the bypass is only as good as the next chokepoint.
routes.source: IEA Oil Market Report, Sep 2026; IEA Strait of Hormuz factsheet, Feb 2026; trade press, Oct 2026

events.title: East-West line ramps to ~5 mb/d
events.text: Saudi Arabia pushed its East-West line to about 5 mb/d (vs ~0.8 mb/d pre-crisis). Port loading at Yanbu, not the pipe, is the binding limit.

events.title: Pumping stations hit
events.text: Drones hit several East-West pumping stations, and satellite images showed fire damage near Al Mesba'ah and Al Dhekra. A US official said the drones came from Iraq. The line was shut on 11 Sep.

events.title: Khurais station hit again
events.text: An AFP source said the line was hit again at a station at Khurais, east of Riyadh, halting flows again. Reuters satellite imagery on 22 Sep showed repairs near Dhekra.

events.title: Tanker hit 63 nm west of Yanbu
events.text: UKMTO: a Bahri tanker was struck by an unknown projectile ~63 nm west of Yanbu. Crew safe. Around 30 tankers near Yanbu sit within Houthi strike range.

events.title: Fujairah: the UAE's exit below Hormuz
events.text: The Habshan–Fujairah line loads tankers in the Gulf of Oman, outside the strait. Capacity is ~1.5 mb/d and port capacity is again the limit.

routes.title: Qatar LNG force majeure: a global gas shock
routes.dateRange: Since Mar 2026; force majeure now extended into mid-Oct; repair of damaged trains pushed to 3-5 years
routes.summary: About 93% of Qatar's and 96% of the UAE's LNG exports pass through Hormuz, roughly 19% of global LNG trade, and none of it has a pipeline bypass. Qatar declared force majeure in March after Iranian strikes damaged the Ras Laffan complex, and the disruption is proving far more durable than oil's: Kpler now estimates Qatari LNG exports will total just 0.6 Mt in October, against a normal cadence of roughly 6-7 Mt/month, even as Gulf crude shipments have recovered to ~80% of pre-war levels. QatarEnergy has pushed back its own repair estimate for the ~17% of capacity knocked out to three to five years, far beyond the 'weeks' timeline floated after June's ceasefire, and force majeure notices to several Asian and European buyers now run into mid-October with no public lift confirmed. The one bright spot is additive, not restorative: the first train of the North Field East expansion is due to begin commissioning in November 2026, targeting initial output in early 2027 — new supply arriving on top of an already-disrupted market rather than replacing the lost trains. European gas (TTF) more than doubled to roughly €70-77/MWh in late August-early September, a three-year high, and US Gulf Coast LNG remains the marginal supplier bidding against both Europe and Asia, which is why Panama Canal slots and Atlantic freight keep mattering so much.
routes.source: Cyprus Mail (12 Oct 2026); meobserver.news (12-13 Oct 2026); Zawya/Reuters Bousso column (Oct 2026); EIA Today in Energy; GIIGNL Annual Report 2026

events.title: Ras Laffan + Mesaieed struck
events.text: Iranian missiles hit Ras Laffan and Mesaieed Industrial City. QatarEnergy halted all LNG production and declared force majeure. ~17% of export capacity is damaged, with repairs taking 3–5 years.

events.title: 1.6 Mt shipped: a third to Kuwait
events.text: September exports were 1.6 Mt, under a quarter of normal. A third went to Kuwait's Al-Zour terminal, which never crosses Hormuz.

events.title: Tanker Acers hit near Ras Laffan
events.text: The Antigua-flagged tanker Acers was hit by multiple projectiles ~50 nm north of Madinat ash Shamal, close to the Ras Laffan LNG complex.

events.title: ~0.6 Mt expected in October
events.text: Kpler expects Qatari LNG exports to drop to ~0.6 Mt in October as attacks on ships intensify (pre-war ≈6.7 Mt a month).

events.title: No bypass for LNG
events.text: ~93% of Qatar's and 96% of the UAE's LNG must pass Hormuz, about 19% of world LNG trade.

routes.title: Red Sea: Houthi attacks resumed, Cape detour continues
routes.dateRange: Since 2024; attacks resumed Feb 2026; Saudi blockade since Jul 2026; airport strikes from Oct 2026
routes.summary: The Houthis' 2025 pause ended at the end of February 2026, when they announced renewed attacks on Red Sea shipping, linked to the strikes on Iran. In July they declared a complete naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, aimed squarely at the oil Saudi Arabia was rerouting to Yanbu to avoid Hormuz, and in September seized the port of Mokha plus Mayun (Perim) island and the Hanish islands, giving them effective control of both shores of Bab-el-Mandeb despite a Saudi-backed counter-offensive claim on 4 October. The conflict escalated sharply in early October: Houthi missiles struck Riyadh's airport twice (9–10 Oct), killing at least 13 people, and the group has warned airlines and travelers to avoid all Saudi airports and airspace except Mecca and Medina — widening this from a shipping chokepoint into an aviation one too. Bab-el-Mandeb traffic has fallen to roughly 32 ships/day from a pre-blockade ~50. Around 30 tankers near Yanbu sit within Houthi strike range, and most Asia–Europe tankers and container ships still go round the Cape, adding about 10–14 days. That ties up ships and lifts freight rates on every route, not just this one.
routes.source: CNN (10 Oct 2026); PBS NewsHour (2026); Reuters via aaj.tv (11 Aug 2026); CNBC (22 Jul 2026); CFR; Lloyd's List Intelligence Red Sea brief (Aug 2026)

events.text: The 2025 pause ends: the Houthis announce renewed attacks on Red Sea shipping, linked to the strikes on Iran.

events.text: UKMTO: a cargo ship reported being 'under attack by unknown armed assailants' 30 nm south-west of Hodeidah. Ship and crew safe.

events.title: Saudi tankers Encelia & Layla
events.text: The Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi tankers after declaring a total naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, aimed at oil diverted to Yanbu.

events.title: Tihamah hit, 6 killed
events.text: Two ballistic missiles hit the cargo ship Tihamah in Bab-el-Mandeb, killing four sailors. A second strike on a Yemeni coast-guard rescue boat killed two rescuers.

events.title: Tanker hit 63 nm W of Yanbu
events.text: UKMTO: a Bahri tanker was struck by a projectile ~63 nm west of Yanbu, far north of the usual attack zone.

events.text: Houthi forces seized the port of Mokha on the Red Sea coast.

events.title: Perim island seized
events.text: Perim island, inside the Bab-el-Mandeb strait itself, taken by Houthi forces.

events.title: Hanish islands seized
events.text: The Hanish islands in the southern Red Sea, astride the shipping lane, seized.

events.title: Saudi-backed counter-offensive
events.text: Saudi-backed Yemeni forces launched a counter-offensive and claimed control of the strait. The situation is fluid.

events.title: 12 attacks in the south
events.text: 12 Houthi attacks or attempted attacks on commercial vessels in the southern Red Sea since July. Most Asia–Europe tankers and boxships still go round the Cape (+10–14 days).

routes.title: Panama Canal: El Niño drought caps transits
routes.dateRange: Restrictions Aug–Sep 2026; eased 15 Oct as rainfall recovered
routes.summary: A severe El Niño cut rainfall in the canal watershed roughly 34% below average from May to August, prompting the canal authority's first daily transit cap since the 2023–24 crisis: 34 ships a day from 3 September, then 32 from 15 September (versus a normal ~36). September rainfall came in close to average, so the expected 1 October draught cut to 47.5 ft was postponed, and as of 15 October the canal eased instead of tightening: Neopanamax daily transits rose from 9 to 10 (33 total) and the Neopanamax maximum draught rose to 49.0 ft (14.94 m), both now in effect. The watershed deficit hasn't fully closed, and the canal administrator has warned this El Niño could run longer than past cycles, so September–November rainfall will still decide whether slots get cut again in the January–March 2027 dry season. Demand stayed unusually high through the squeeze: laden LNG transits hit a two-year high in June as US cargoes chased Asian prices after the loss of Qatari supply, and an LPG carrier slot sold at auction for a record $5.3 million on 1 September.
routes.source: Ship & Bunker (30 Sep 2026); Seatrade Maritime (2026); S&P Global Commodity Insights (Jul 2026); Hellenic Shipping News (Sep 2026)

events.title: Rainfall −34%
events.text: A severe El Niño cut rainfall in the canal watershed ~34% below average. Gatun Lake feeds every lock transit.
events.source: Panama Canal Authority via Marine Insight (2026)

events.text: US LNG cargoes chased Asian prices after Qatar's outage.

events.text: An LPG carrier paid a record $5.3m for a transit slot. VLGC freight hit record highs.

events.text: First daily transit cap since the 2023–24 crisis (normal ~36), plus draught cuts.

routes.title: Russian crude: shadow fleet to India and China
routes.summary: Russia ships roughly 3.8–4.1 mb/d of crude by sea; China takes ~51% and India ~38%. The sanctioned 'shadow' fleet's share has kept climbing: from almost half of Russia's seaborne oil in March 2026 to 52% by August, per CREA, carried mostly on tankers over 15 years old. Western governments have now sanctioned over 650 tankers, and Washington added direct sanctions on Rosneft and Lukoil in October 2025, but enforcement gaps persist — re-flagging to Russia's own international register has accelerated, and some already-listed tankers keep loading regardless. India's imports of Russian crude doubled month on month in March, as Gulf supply was shut in. With the Red Sea unsafe, Baltic cargoes to India increasingly go round Africa.
routes.source: CREA monthly analysis (Sep 2026); KSE Institute Russian Oil Tracker (May 2026)

events.text: Russia ships ~3.8–4.1 mb/d of crude by sea. In March 2026 almost half moved on sanctioned shadow tankers, 92% of them over 15 years old.

events.text: Old, under-insured tankers pass the Danish straits and the Channel, a growing concern for coastal states. The West has now sanctioned 651 tankers.

routes.title: Petrochemicals: China flips from PE/PP importer to exporter
routes.summary: From the original Tricon-prep version of this map, kept because it is a demand-side story, not a transport one. China's PE/PP imports hit record lows in April 2026 while its PE exports hit record highs (+122% YoY), squeezing the export markets that ~3.3 Mt/yr of new US Gulf Coast PE capacity (Shell, Baystar, Nova, Dow) built since 2023 was counting on.

events.title: Record PE exports (+122% YoY)
events.text: China's PE/PP imports hit record lows while PE exports hit record highs.

events.title: New US Gulf PE capacity squeezed
events.text: ~3.3 Mt/yr of new US Gulf Coast PE capacity (Shell, Baystar, Nova, Dow) loses export markets to Chinese material.
